query: Consider the following context: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for next-generation nuclear applications, particularly fusion reactors, due to their excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In that context, which material can be used for low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors, and why?

decision.trend: The research trend is focused on developing refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with improved high-temperature mechanical properties, irradiation resistance, and low activation for nuclear applications. The studies have explored various processing routes, such as arc-melting, spark plasma sintering, and laser powder bed fusion, to produce HEAs with optimized microstructures and properties. The results have shown that HEAs can exhibit superior radiation resistance, high-temperature strength, and ductility, making them promising candidates for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved problem is to develop a low-activation structural material that can withstand the harsh environment of high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors. The current materials have limitations in terms of their high-temperature mechanical properties, irradiation resistance, and activation levels. The development of refractory HEAs with optimized properties is an active area of research, and further studies are needed to overcome the existing challenges and achieve the required performance.
decision.why: The next step is to investigate the effect of adding minor alloying elements to refractory HEAs to further improve their high-temperature mechanical properties, irradiation resistance, and low activation. This approach has been shown to be effective in optimizing the properties of HEAs in previous studies. The addition of minor alloying elements can help to refine the microstructure, improve the strength and ductility, and reduce the activation levels of the HEAs, making them more suitable for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
